The accused in C.C.No.400 of 2000 on the files of the Court of the Judicial Magistrate of First Class,
Vaikom, has filed this revision petition challenging the concurrent finding of conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Section 16 (1A) (i) r/w Section 7(i) r/w Rule 2 (ia) (a) (f)
and (m) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act.

entities.text:
Judicial Magistrate of First Class,
Vaikom
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
2. Heard.
3.

The prosecution allegation can be briefly stated thus:-
On 29.10.1999 at 11 a.m., PW2, the Food Inspector purchased 600 grams of cowpeas from the shop of the accused.
After sampling as per the rules, one sample was sent to the Public Analyst for analysis.

The Public Analyst, after analysis, submitted Ext.P16 report stating that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for food grain under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules and was therefore adulterated.
It was further stated in Ext.P16 that the sample contained insect damaged matter, which was not less than 23% and was therefore unfit for human consumption.
4. Before the trial Court, PW1 to PW7 were examined and Exts.P1 to P21 were marked for the prosecution.
DW1 was examined for the revision petitioner.

5. The learned counsel for the revision petitioner has submitted that since no laboratory for the analysis of the food item was defined and no validated method of analysis was prescribed as per the mandate of Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act, Ext.P16 cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was adulterated.
The learned counsel for the revision petitioner relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument.

entities.text: Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
6. In this case, admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee)
and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act.

Therefore, Ext. P16 report of analysis cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased in this case was adulterated in view of the decision of the Apex court in V.K. Pankajakshannair Aged 56 Years vs State Of Kerala on 14 January, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/108937184/
2

entities.text: V.K. Pankajakshannair Aged 56 Years vs State Of Kerala
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Pepsico India Holdings (supra).

It was held by the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra)
that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report and the accused was entitled to get acquittal.

In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court acquitted the accused.
The matter was referred to a Division Bench and the Division Bench also affirmed the said decision, submitted by the learned counsel for the petitioner and the learned Public Prosecutor.

Even otherwise, in view of the decision in Pepsico India Holdings (supra), the conviction in this case cannot be sustained as no laboratory was notified and no validated method of analysis was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee) and (hh) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.

In the result, this revision petition stands allowed setting aside the conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Section 16 (1A) (i) r/w Section 7(i) r/w Rule 2 (ia) (a)
(f) and (m) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act and the revision petitioner is acquitted for the said offence.
